title: Tree Data Structures
html:
A tree is a non-linear, hierarchical data structure: one root node with children, each of which is the root of a smaller tree. Folders, HTML documents, organisation charts, expression parsers, database indexes and every search tree and heap are trees — and most tree algorithms are five-line recursions once you see the structure.

Tree — a collection of nodes connected by edges such that there is exactly one root and every other node has exactly one parent — so there are no cycles and n nodes always have n − 1 edges. A binary tree is a tree in which every node has at most two children, called left and right.

Terminology

TermMeaningIn the sample tree
NodeOne element: a key plus links to its children10, 20, … (8 nodes)
EdgeThe link from a parent to a child; a tree of n nodes has n − 1 edges7 edges
RootThe topmost node — the only node without a parent10
Parent / childThe node directly above / directly below along an edge50 is the parent of 70 and 80
SiblingsChildren of the same parent70 and 80; 20 and 30
Leaf (external node)A node with no children40, 70, 80, 60
Internal nodeA node with at least one child10, 20, 30, 50
SubtreeA node together with all its descendants — itself a treethe subtree rooted at 20 is 20, 40, 50, 70, 80
AncestorsAll nodes on the path from a node up to the rootancestors of 70: 50, 20, 10
DescendantsAll nodes in a node's subtree except itselfdescendants of 20: 40, 50, 70, 80
Degree of a nodeNumber of children (at most 2 in a binary tree)degree of 20 is 2, of 30 is 1, of 40 is 0
Depth of a nodeNumber of edges from the root down to the nodedepth of 70 is 3, of the root is 0
LevelAll nodes at the same depth (level 0 = root)level 2 is 40 50 60
Height of a nodeNumber of edges on the longest downward path to a leaf (a leaf has height 0)height of 20 is 2
Height of the treeHeight of the root3 edges — or 4 if you count nodes on that path (the convention of these notes)
Key point

Two height conventions exist. Counting edges, the sample tree has height 3 and an empty tree has height −1. Counting nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path (what the notes and GeeksforGeeks do, and what the height() code below returns), it has height 4 and an empty tree has height 0. Interviewers accept either — just say which one you use.

Where trees are used

Trees are the natural representation of anything hierarchical, and the basis of most fast search structures.

Hierarchical data

Organisation structures, folder / file systems, XML and HTML documents (the DOM), nested JSON objects, class inheritance in OOP.

Binary search tree

Keys kept in sorted order with O(log n) search, insert and delete — std::map, TreeMap (next topic).

Binary heap

A complete binary tree in an array; the priority queue behind heap sort, Dijkstra and schedulers (topic after next).

B and B+ trees

Wide, shallow search trees that keep disk reads to a minimum — the indexes of every relational database.

Spanning and shortest-path trees

Prim's and Kruskal's minimum spanning trees, Dijkstra's shortest-path tree — the backbone of routing in computer networks.

Parse and expression trees

Compilers turn source code into a syntax tree; (a + b) * c is a tree with * at the root.

Special-purpose variations you will meet later in DSA Advanced:

VariationWhat it is for
Trie (prefix tree)Strings keyed character by character — autocomplete, spell check, IP routing tables
Suffix treeAll suffixes of a text — substring search in O(m)
Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick tree)Prefix sums with O(log n) point updates in a plain array
Segment treeRange queries (sum, min, max) with O(log n) updates

Kinds of binary tree

The same n keys can form very different binary trees. The shape decides the height, and the height decides how fast everything runs — so the special shapes have names.

KindRuleWhy it matters
Full (strict / proper)Every node has either 0 or 2 childrenLeaves = internal nodes + 1; expression trees are full
CompleteEvery level is completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to rightCan be stored in an array with no gaps — this is what a binary heap is
PerfectAll internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves are on the same levelExactly 2^h − 1 nodes for height h (in nodes); the densest possible tree
BalancedHeight is O(log n) — e.g. AVL: left and right heights differ by at most 1 at every nodeGuarantees O(log n) search, insert and delete in a BST
Degenerate (skewed)Every node has exactly one childHeight n − 1: it behaves like a linked list, every operation becomes O(n)

Useful facts (height counted in nodes): level l holds at most 2^l nodes; a tree of height h holds at most 2^h − 1 nodes; therefore n nodes need height at least ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉. A perfect tree is always complete and full; a complete tree need not be full (node 3 above has one child); a full tree need not be complete.

Binary tree node and building the sample tree

A binary tree is a linked data structure, like a linked list with two links. Each node stores a key and pointers to its left and right child; a missing child is None / nullptr / null. The tree is identified by its root pointer alone — there is no separate container object. Every program in this topic starts by building the sample tree with this node class.

Key point

Building a tree by hand like this is fine for examples. Real code builds trees by insertion (a BST), from an array (a heap, or a level-order array with -1 for missing nodes) or by parsing input.

Tree traversals

Traversing means visiting every node exactly once. A list has one natural order; a tree has several, and each one is useful for something.

TraversalOrderSample tree givesTypical use
Inorder (depth-first)Left subtree → Root → Right subtree40 20 70 50 80 10 30 60Sorted output of a binary search tree
Preorder (depth-first)Root → Left → Right10 20 40 50 70 80 30 60Copying / serialising a tree, prefix expressions
Postorder (depth-first)Left → Right → Root40 70 80 50 20 60 30 10Deleting a tree (children before parent), folder sizes, postfix expressions
Level order (breadth-first)Level 0, then level 1, … left to right10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80Shortest paths, printing by level, anything that needs closest first
Idea

All three depth-first traversals are the same recursion — visit(root.left), visit(root.right) and print the root — in a different order. The names say where the root goes: pre-order before the children, in-order in between, post-order after. Each recursive call handles one node and makes two calls, so the total work is O(n); the recursion stack is as deep as the tree, so auxiliary space is O(h).

Inorder traversal

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 20 70 50 80 10 30 60

Recurse into the left subtree, print the node, recurse into the right subtree. On a BST this prints the keys in sorted order, which is why inorder is the traversal you will use most.

Time O(n)Space O(h) recursion stack — O(n) for a skewed tree, O(log n) when balanced
Pitfall

The notes' comment Auxiliary space Θ(n) is the worst case only. The stack holds one frame per ancestor of the current node, so its depth is the height h; it reaches n only for a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree.

Preorder traversal

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 20 40 50 70 80 30 60

Print the node first, then its subtrees. Preorder lists every node before its descendants, so writing a tree out in preorder (with markers for missing children) is enough to rebuild it — this is how trees are serialised and copied.

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Postorder traversal

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 70 80 50 20 60 30 10

Both subtrees first, the node last. Postorder visits children before their parent, so it is the order for anything that must finish the parts before the whole: freeing a tree's nodes, computing directory sizes, evaluating an expression tree.

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Key point

In C++ the destructor of a tree is a postorder traversal: delete the left subtree, delete the right subtree, then the node — deleting the node first would lose the pointers to its children.

Height of a binary tree

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 4 (nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path 10 → 20 → 50 → 70)
Input: an empty tree
Output: 0

Idea

The height of a tree is one more than the taller of its two subtrees. That is the whole algorithm: recurse into both children, take the maximum, add 1. The base case — an empty subtree — has height 0 under the node-counting convention.

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Key point

To count edges instead, return -1 for an empty tree; the sample tree then has height 3. The + 1 stays the same.

Print nodes at distance K from the root

Example

Input: the sample tree, K = 2
Output: 40 50 60
Input: K = 1
Output: 20 30
Input: K = 3
Output: 70 80

Idea

A node is at distance K from the root exactly when it is at distance K − 1 from one of the root's children. So pass K down the recursion, decrementing at each level; when it reaches 0, the current node is one of the answers. Nothing needs to come back up — the recursion just needs to reach depth K.

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Key point

The recursion visits at most all nodes down to depth K, so it is O(n) in the worst case but stops early for small K. Nodes at distance K from the root are exactly level K — the level-order traversal below produces the same groups without recursion.

Level order traversal (breadth-first)

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80
Input: the tree 3 → 4 → 5 (each the left child of the previous)
Output: 3 4 5

Idea

Recursion naturally goes deep. To go wide — whole level before the next — use a queue: start with the root, and every time you dequeue a node, enqueue its children. Because a queue is FIFO, all of level d is dequeued before anything from level d + 1, which was enqueued later.

1
Start
Push the root into an empty queue.
2
Loop while the queue is not empty
Pop the front node and print it.
3
Enqueue children
Push its left child, then its right child (if they exist) — they will be visited after everything already in the queue.
Time O(n)Space O(w) — the widest level, up to n/2 nodes for a perfect tree

Level by level. Interviewers usually want each level on its own line. Record the queue's size at the start of each round: exactly that many nodes belong to the current level, so pop just those, then start the next line.

Time O(n)Space O(w)
Pitfall

Using a plain list / array as the queue and removing from the front (list.pop(0), Array.shift()) makes every dequeue O(n) and the traversal O(n²). Use collections.deque, std::queue, ArrayDeque, or an index into the array as above.

Size of a binary tree

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 8
Input: an empty tree
Output: 0

Idea

The size of a tree is the size of the left subtree plus the size of the right subtree plus one for the root. Same shape as height(), with + instead of max.

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Key point

Every node is visited once and does O(1) work, hence O(n) time. An iterative version is level order with a counter — the recursion is just shorter.

Maximum value in a binary tree

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 80
Input: an empty tree
Output: -inf (no maximum)

Idea

The maximum of a tree is the largest of three things: the root's key, the maximum of the left subtree and the maximum of the right subtree. The base case returns −∞ so that an empty subtree never wins. A plain binary tree has no ordering, so every node must be looked at — unlike a BST, where the maximum is simply the rightmost node.

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

Returning 0 for an empty subtree is wrong as soon as all keys are negative. Use the smallest possible value (-math.inf, INT_MIN, Integer.MIN_VALUE, -Infinity) as the base case — the same trick gives getMin with +∞ and min.

Recursion on trees: the pattern

Height, size, maximum, and most other tree problems have the same three-line shape — remember it and you can derive the others in an interview.

1
Base case
if root is None: return <identity> — 0 for counting, 0/-1 for height, −∞ for max, +∞ for min, True for is valid.
2
Recurse
Solve the problem for root.left and root.right — trust the recursion to return the right answer for each subtree.
3
Combine
Mix the two answers with the root: max(l, r) + 1, l + r + 1, max(key, l, r), l and r and <condition on root>.
ProblemBase caseCombine
Height0max(l, r) + 1
Size0l + r + 1
Maximum−∞max(key, l, r)
Sum of keys0l + r + key
Count leaves0; a leaf returns 1l + r
Is balancedTruel and r and |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1

Interview Q&A

What is the difference between a binary tree and a binary search tree?

A binary tree only limits every node to at most two children — the keys can be anywhere. A binary search tree adds an ordering invariant: every key in a node's left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger. That invariant is what makes search O(h) instead of O(n).

Why is the height of a tree so important?

Almost every operation walks one root-to-leaf path, so it costs O(h). For a balanced tree h = O(log n); for a skewed tree h = n − 1, and the tree degrades into a linked list. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) exist purely to keep h logarithmic.

Which traversal would you use to delete every node of a tree, and why?

Postorder: both children are freed before the parent, so no pointer to a child is ever lost. Preorder would free the parent — and the links to its children — first.

How do you get the inorder sequence without recursion?

Use an explicit stack: walk left pushing every node, pop one and print it, then move to its right child and repeat. It is the same O(n) time and O(h) space, but the stack is yours instead of the call stack — useful in languages with a small recursion limit (Python stops at about 1000 frames).

Is level order traversal depth-first or breadth-first, and what data structure does it need?

Breadth-first — it finishes a level before starting the next. It needs a queue; the three depth-first traversals need a stack (the call stack when written recursively). Space is O(w) for the widest level versus O(h) for depth-first; for a perfect tree the last level holds about n/2 nodes, so BFS can use far more memory.

Can you rebuild a binary tree from its traversals?

From inorder plus preorder (or inorder plus postorder), yes: the first preorder element is the root, its position in the inorder sequence splits the inorder into the left and right subtrees, and you recurse. Preorder plus postorder alone is not enough — a node with a single child is ambiguous. A single traversal with null markers is also enough, which is how serialisation works.
